summary: Specifies a generic mechanism to extend IGMPv3 and Multicast Listener Discovery version 2 (MLDv2) using a list of TLVs (Type, Length, Value). That makes it easier to add new information to these multicast group membership messages in the future. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: These messages are short forms with no spare space. This adds a place at the end to attach extra labeled notes, each saying what it is and how long it is.

questions: what is tlv extension for mldv2
what is the e-bit in igmp and mld
what is the igmp mld no-op tlv
how are igmp mld tlvs validated
subtitle: A generic list of type-length-value extensions for IGMPv3 and MLDv2 multicast membership messages.

tldr.problem: IGMPv3 and MLDv2 messages have fixed formats with no clean way to carry new kinds of information.
tldr.mechanism: A previously reserved bit, the E-bit, signals that the Additional Data section holds a list of TLVs (Type, Length, Value), with extension types kept in a new IANA registry.
tldr.outcome: Other documents can now define new extension types for queries and reports. The RFC itself defines only a No-op TLV, and expects adoption to be slow.

today: RFC 9279 is a Proposed Standard from August 2022. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself expects adoption to be slow, because IGMP and MLD implementations rarely change.

sections.title: Why Extend IGMPv3 and MLDv2
sections.content:
This RFC defines a generic way to extend IGMPv3 and MLDv2 messages so they can carry information beyond what the current formats hold. It does this by allowing a list of TLVs in the Additional Data section of those messages. It also defines a registry for the TLV types. Other documents will define specific types and what they mean.

The extension is used only when at least one TLV is to be added to a message. It also applies to the lightweight versions of IGMPv3 and MLDv2 defined in RFC 5790. When the mechanism is used, the TLVs replace the Additional Data section defined in IGMPv3 and MLDv2.
sections.eli5: Imagine a form with no blank lines left for notes. This RFC adds a spot at the bottom where anyone can staple on extra labeled notes.

sections.title: The Extension Format
sections.content:
A previously reserved bit in each IGMPv3 and MLDv2 header, the E-bit, signals that the extension is present. It MUST be 1 when the extension is there and 0 otherwise. When it is used, the Additional Data is a variable number of TLVs, and it MUST contain at least one.

Each TLV has an Extension Type of 2 octets, an Extension Length of 2 octets, and an Extension Value. The length counts the octets of the value that follows, and may be zero. The next TLV follows immediately, with no alignment or padding.

IGMPv3 and MLDv2 messages are designed to fit within the network MTU to avoid fragmentation. With this extension, the number of records in each Report SHOULD be kept small enough that the whole message, including the TLVs, fits within the MTU.
sections.eli5: A little flag at the top says whether extra notes are stuck on. Each note has a label, a size and then its contents, and notes sit one right after another.

sections.title: Where the E-bit Sits in Each Message
sections.content:
The RFC shows the extension in four message types. In the MLDv2 Query (Type 130) and the IGMPv3 Membership Query (Type 0x11), the E-bit is the first bit of the byte that also holds a reserved field, the S flag and the QRV field, followed by QQIC and the Number of Sources. In the MLDv2 Report (Type 143) and the IGMPv3 Membership Report (Type 0x22), the E-bit is the first bit of the field that precedes the record count.

In every case the Extension follows the last source address (in queries) or the last record (in reports).
sections.eli5: In each kind of message the flag lives in the same spot near the start, and the extra notes always go at the very end.

sections.title: The No-op TLV
sections.content:
The only type defined here is the No-op TLV, with type 0. It MUST be ignored during processing. It may be used to check that the extension mechanism has been implemented correctly. Because there is no alignment requirement, it is not needed for padding.

Its value can be arbitrary data, but the number of octets used MUST match the specified length.
sections.eli5: A No-op note is a note that says nothing on purpose. It is useful for checking that notes are being read and skipped correctly.

sections.title: Processing and Validation
sections.content:
The procedure applies only when the E-bit is set. If validation of the TLVs fails, the entire Additional Data field MUST be ignored, as IGMPv3 and MLDv2 already specify. Validation fails unless all of these hold:

  • At least one TLV is present.
  • No data follows the last TLV. A parser walks the TLVs until fewer than four octets are left in the IP payload; if any octets remain, validation fails.
  • The total length of the Extension does not exceed the rest of the IP payload. Only the Extension Length fields are examined for this check.

TLVs with unsupported Extension Types MUST be ignored. Future documents that define a new type MUST specify any extra processing and validation, which is applied only after the general validation succeeds.
sections.eli5: If the stack of notes is broken, for example a note claims to be longer than the page, the receiver throws the whole stack away. A note it does not understand is simply skipped.

sections.title: Applicability and Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
IGMP and MLD implementations, especially on hosts, rarely change, so adoption is expected to be slow and new TLVs may take a long time to be supported. For that reason, defining new extension types should not be taken lightly. Implementations that do not support the mechanism ignore it, as IGMPv3 and MLDv2 specify.

A document defining a new type MUST say when it is used, including which message types, and what to do if it shows up in the wrong kind of message. Authors should also consider partial support by hosts or routers on the same link, and any dependencies between the new type and existing ones. The mechanism does not apply when hosts or routers send older-version messages.
sections.eli5: Old devices will just not read the new notes. So anyone inventing a new kind of note has to make sure things still work when some devices ignore it.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of IGMPv3 and MLDv2 also apply. Because TLVs are variable in number, implementations must not read past the packet boundary, since an attacker could specify a TLV whose length exceeds it. An implementation could also add a large number of minimal TLVs to a message to raise the cost of processing it, which would magnify a denial-of-service attack.

IANA created the "IGMP/MLD Extension Types" registry, common to IGMP and MLD, with the "IETF Review" procedure. Type 0 is the No-op, types 1 to 65533 are unassigned, and types 65534 and 65535 are for experimental use, which should be confined to closed environments.
sections.eli5: A liar could write a note that claims to be huge, or pile on thousands of tiny notes to keep a receiver busy, so receivers must be careful when reading.

fields.name: Extension Type
fields.desc: Identifies the type in the IGMP/MLD Extension Types registry.

fields.name: Extension Length
fields.desc: Length in octets of the value that follows; may be zero.
